title: The Physics of Topological Defects in Glasses
authors: Arabinda Bera, Peter Schall, Timothy W. Sirk, Vijayakumar Chikkadi, Alessio Zaccone
abstract: Topological defects play a central role in the mechanical behavior of crystalline materials, yet their relevance to amorphous solids has only recently begun to emerge. Over the last few years, theoretical, computational, and experimental studies have revealed the presence of well-defined topological invariants in vibrational eigenmodes, non-affine displacement fields, and deformation-induced vector fields of glasses. These defects have been shown to correlate strongly with soft spots, localized plastic rearrangements, yielding, and shear-band formation, suggesting a new perspective on the microscopic origins of plasticity in disordered materials. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent developments in the rapidly growing field of topological defects in glasses. We discuss the underlying theoretical concepts, including Burgers vectors, non-affine plasticity, vibrational modes, and topological invariants, and review recent numerical and experimental advances. Finally, we assess the current achievements, limitations, and open questions, and discuss future directions toward a unified topological description of plasticity and mechanical failure in amorphous solids.
summary: This review synthesizes recent work showing that topological defects govern mechanical failure in amorphous solids. By analyzing fields derived from particle displacements and vibrational modes, the authors demonstrate that singularities like vortices correlate precisely with yielding transitions. This suggests topology offers a powerful, universal descriptor for plasticity beyond traditional structural models.
main_problem: The review aims to establish a unified topological description for plasticity and mechanical failure in amorphous solids (glasses), extending concepts from crystalline defects.
main_result: Topological defects, such as vortices and hedgehog defects derived from non-affine displacements or vibrational modes, show strong correlations with soft spots, yielding, and shear-band formation in glasses.
method: The study combines theoretical frameworks (e.g., STZ theory, non-affine elasticity) with computational analysis of topological invariants calculated on continuous fields derived from simulations.
model_or_system: The physical system is amorphous solids, including metallic and colloidal glasses, studied across various states like jammed or yielding regimes. The analysis focuses on the structural disorder inherent to these materials.
key_observables: Topological invariants (winding numbers, hedgehog charges), non-affine displacement fields ($D_{2,	ext{min}}$), low-frequency vibrational modes, and defect density ($	ext{NHTD}$).
important_parameters: Shear strain ($\gamma$), critical fraction of non-affine particles ($p_c$), and the frequency spectrum ($\omega$) of vibrations.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that topological structures provide a robust, universal language to describe mechanical failure in disordered systems, analogous to dislocations in crystals.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate defect visualization (vortices/hedgehog defects) in 2D and 3D fields derived from non-affine displacements and vibrational modes. Key figures correlate the density of these topological defects with the onset of yielding or shear localization.
paper_structure: The review progresses by contrasting crystalline defect theory with amorphous systems, introducing concepts like non-affine motion and soft spots, and culminating in a systematic analysis showing how topological charges characterize plasticity during mechanical loading.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter mechanics, the reliance on characterizing system states via global topological invariants (like winding numbers) is mathematically analogous to methods used in quantum field theory or analyzing entanglement structures in many-body systems.
